tier_reason: OVERVIEW.md's Primitive Summary gives the fastest-external geomeans for every listed primitive (sha256 1.27x, sha3-256 2.28x, blake2b256 1.07x, and so on) from the 2026-08-18 eight-host Linux snapshot at commit 7eb44e9. The benchmark code is public (benches/sha2.rs, benches/sha3.rs, benches/blake2.rs, Criterion). The repo at that commit pins rust-toolchain nightly-2026-07-17 and sets -C target-cpu=native in .cargo/config.toml, and the bench profile uses opt-level=3, fat LTO and codegen-units=1. CPU families are named per host.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Fastest-external geomean on the 2026-08-18 eight-host Linux scorecard (ratio = external_time / rscrypto_time; >1x means rscrypto is faster): sha256 1.27x (104 rows, W/T/L 44/46/14; all-pairs geomean 1.60x), sha384 1.30x, sha512 1.29x, sha3-224 2.27x, sha3-256 2.28x, sha3-384 2.35x, sha3-512 2.38x, blake2b256 1.07x (all-pairs 1.31x), blake2b512 1.08x (all-pairs 1.33x), blake2s256 1.11x, blake2s128 1.13x. The page gives no per-primitive medians. The 1.60x, 1.31x and 1.33x figures that the original record labelled medians are all-pairs geomeans.
corrections.baseline: Fastest external Rust implementation per case. SHA-256/384/512: RustCrypto sha2, aws-lc-rs (AWS-LC) and ring. SHA3-224/256/384/512: RustCrypto sha3. BLAKE2: RustCrypto blake2, plus dryoc for BLAKE2b.
corrections.hardware: 2026-08-18 eight-host Linux scorecard: AMD Zen4, AMD Zen5, AWS Graviton3, AWS Graviton4, IBM Power10, IBM z16 (s390x), Intel Ice Lake and Intel Sapphire Rapids. The page names microarchitecture families only, with no exact SKUs or instance types for this snapshot. The RISC-V host did not contribute, and there are no Windows hosts in this scorecard.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page for the 2026-08-18 snapshot. At the snapshot commit 7eb44e9 the repo pins rust-toolchain nightly-2026-07-17 and sets RUSTFLAGS -C target-cpu=native in .cargo/config.toml (with +lse on aarch64) for Linux x86_64/aarch64. The bench profile inherits release: opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1, panic=abort. The harness is Criterion. Rust 1.98.1 and 1.99.0-nightly were the toolchains of the separate 2026-09-14 run, whose ratios are not in the scorecard.
corrections.workload: Criterion benchmarks (benches/sha2.rs, benches/sha3.rs, benches/blake2.rs) of one-shot and streaming SHA-224/256/384/512, SHA3-224/256/384/512 and BLAKE2b/BLAKE2s hashing across input sizes. They ran on the 2026-08-18 eight-host Linux matrix: x86_64 AMD/Intel, aarch64 Graviton3/4, ppc64le Power10 and s390x z16.
corrections.caveats: The baseline is the fastest competing Rust crate or binding per case. For SHA-2 it includes aws-lc-rs (AWS-LC, OpenSSL/BoringSSL lineage) and ring, but OpenSSL itself was not tested, so baseline_in_list stays false. OVERVIEW.md withdraws its ML-KEM and Argon2 comparisons. It also flags historical BLAKE2 host-overhead and parameter rows as duplicates of the main one-shot cases without recomputing ratios, so the BLAKE2 row counts and geomeans may include duplicated cases. The scorecard is a historical snapshot of commit 7eb44e9. The raw results.txt files it cites under benchmark_results/2026-08-18/ are no longer in the repo. Compiler flags for the cross-built POWER and s390x hosts are not stated.

notes: The original record mixed in hardware and toolchains from the separate 2026-09-14 run (c8a/c8i/c9g plus Windows), which the page says is not folded into the scorecard; I replaced them with the 2026-08-18 hosts. GitHub's API reports the license as Apache-2.0, but Cargo.toml declares MIT OR Apache-2.0 and both LICENSE files are present. I kept tier A because code, toolchain pin, flags and CPU families are all recoverable at the snapshot commit.

tier_reason: PERFORMANCE.md and the README compare the sha2x4 backend with the scalar backend, which is literally a loop over Go stdlib crypto/sha256.Sum256 (scalar.go). The numbers are 57.58M vs 21.55M hashes/s at n=6144, about 2.6x, and 2.57-2.67x across thermal states. Benchmark code is public (bench_test.go BenchmarkHash33), and Go 1.22.5, GOMAXPROCS=1, -count=8 median and Apple M3 are all stated.

corrections.baseline: Go standard library crypto/sha256 (sha256.Sum256 called once per message; this is the package's 'scalar' backend)
corrections.caveats: This is a very new single-author project with 0 stars and no independent verification. The numbers come from the author's local smoke benchmark. The workload is narrow: fixed 33-byte messages. The win is arm64-only, because amd64 has no SIMD backend yet and runs scalar crypto/sha256, so there is no speedup on x86. The stdlib baseline itself already uses the ARMv8 SHA-2 instructions on Apple Silicon, so the gain comes from 4-way multi-buffer interleaving, not from hardware SHA versus software SHA.

notes: All numbers match the README and PERFORMANCE.md. The last commit was 2026-05-31, about 4 months ago, so I changed maintenance_status to active. The MIT license and 0 stars are confirmed by the GitHub API.

tier_reason: These are first-party README runs of the public src/bench.c, built with HAVE_OPENSSL=1 and src/Makefile using -O3. The OpenSSL comparisons use an unnamed x86-64 CPU and an ambiguously named board, and give no compiler or OpenSSL versions. That is first-party numbers with partial methodology, so tier C. Tier B would need a peer-reviewed or independent suite.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Unnamed x86-64 CPU without SHA extensions: OpenSSL SHA256() called one message at a time takes 30.519 ms, vs 6.519 ms for avx_x8 (AVX2, 8 blocks per call). That is about 4.7x (derived from page data); the README says '5 times faster'. Banana Pi BPI-R3, which the README describes as RISC-V: OpenSSL takes 465.372 ms vs 109.428 ms for riscv_zbb_x1, about 4.25x (derived from page data); the README says '450% improvement'. The Cascade Lake avx_x16 figure of 2.413 ms vs about 28.8 ms for a single block is about 12x, but against the library's own x1 kernel, not OpenSSL. The Go-binding benchmarks are about 6-11x faster than Prysm's earlier Go implementation (derived from page data), also not OpenSSL.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc/gas (Apple clang on Apple Silicon) via src/Makefile with CFLAGS -g -Wall -Werror -O3; RISC-V builds add -march=rv64gc_zbb_zk. HAVE_OPENSSL=1 links the system OpenSSL. The compiler and OpenSSL versions are not stated.
corrections.hardware: Direct OpenSSL comparisons: an unnamed x86-64 CPU without SHA extensions (AVX2-capable), and a Banana Pi BPI-R3 that the README describes as having a RISC-V processor. Rows without OpenSSL: an unnamed Cascade Lake AVX-512 host and a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B. Go comparisons against Prysm: AMD Ryzen 5 3600, Intel Core i5-3570 and i5-7200U.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 42 stars. The status-im/nimbus-eth2 source references hashtree through its Nim bindings. Prysm's go.mod depends on the separate Go-assembly port prysmaticlabs/gohashtree (25 stars), not on C bindings of this repo.
corrections.caveats: Both direct OpenSSL comparisons come from underspecified hardware: an x86 CPU identified only as lacking SHA extensions, and a board the README calls a 'Banana Pi BPI-R3 with a RISC-V processor'. The OpenSSL case calls the one-shot SHA256() once per 64-byte message, single-buffer, while hashtree takes many blocks per call. The gap is therefore mainly multi-buffer vs single-buffer, and on SHA-NI CPUs, where OpenSSL uses SHA-NI, no same-run OpenSSL number is given. The Cascade Lake and Raspberry Pi rows have no OpenSSL column. No compiler or OpenSSL versions are given.

notes: The benchmark_url on the master branch redirects; the default branch is main. I added the RISC-V row, which the original record missed and which also has a same-run OpenSSL comparison. The BPI-R3 is commonly an ARM (MediaTek) board, so the README's board name may be a typo for a RISC-V Banana Pi; I did not verify this. The usage claim was wrong: Prysm uses the gohashtree Go port, not bindings of this repo.
